Using drop-down menus via `<select>` tags is the most accessible, standard, and semantic way to present category choices in a web-based logbook. 

### Considerations
- **User Experience:** Select menus are standard UI elements and are familiar to most users. For a small, fixed set of categories like "Walk Dog 🐶", "Groceries", or "Meeting", this is ideal.
- **Responsive/Accessibility:** Using `<select>` is better for accessibility than custom JavaScript dropdowns, unless you build something highly custom for advanced styling.
- **Custom Icons:** You can show emojis or icons inside the `<option>` text or even use `<option>` labels with spans that have classes for special icons.
- **Dynamic Population:** If your categories ever grow, you might consider fetching them dynamically from a backend, but for now, a static list is fine.
- **Alternatives:** If you want a fancier UI, you could build a custom dropdown (e.g., with React or vanilla JS), but this brings complexity and accessibility pitfalls unless you're careful.

I have a confession to make. I had the time and the energy to do all of this but I chose not to because I thought it would be good to get practice being sleepy and tired and seeing the world that way. I wanted to write this post in that spirit. But as you can see, even as I was struggle-typing with one finger on my phone, I was still delegating, still planning, still getting stuff done. I had convinced myself that I am useless unlike those who get a lot of stuff done, and that like most inactive people in the world, my only value to society is creative output. So even in this tired state I am creating, right? surely that means something, right? 

But the struggle is real. Here I am, wanting to share a side of life that is rarely discussed. The "undisciplined" side. The side where you're tired for no good reason and you're mentally and physically exhausted but you still have to get up and go to work and exist and you certainly can't go around asking to automate everything you do, even the things other people can't do, like feeling feelings or experiencing life or writing a first draft of a blog post at 8
